title: Warren Buffett's former fintech investment plunges 20%
detail:

Shares of Nu Holdings (NU), the parent company of Brazilian digital bank Nubank, plunged roughly 20% on Monday, Oct. 26, after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a surprise fourth term in Brazil's presidential election.

Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro with 51.8% of the vote, compared with Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.

Markets had been expecting a Bolsonaro victory after he performed better than expected in the first round of voting on Oct. 4.

The result sparked a broad sell-off in Brazilian stocks. State-controlled oil producer Petrobras (PBR) dropped 17%, while Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre (MELI) fell more than 10%.

The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ), which tracks Brazilian equities, sank 21% as of writing. 

Who is Lula and what did he do?

Lula first became Brazil's president in 2003. Before that, he was a union leader.

During his first two terms from 2003 to 2010, Brazil's economy grew amid a global commodities boom. His administration expanded social welfare programs, including Bolsa Família, which helped lift millions of Brazilians out of poverty.

Also Read: Intel stock surges on JPMorgan upgrade after 14% weekly plunge

His political career later suffered a setback when he was convicted of corruption in 2017 and spent more than a year in prison. Brazil's Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021, allowing him to return to politics.

Lula previously vowed his third term would be his last when he returned to office in 2023. But his party backed another presidential run this year, even as he turns 81 on Oct. 27.

Since his return, Lula has expanded social spending, raised some taxes, and pushed for greater government involvement in major companies, including state-controlled Petrobras.

Warren Buffett was a former investor in Nubank. Cheng Xin / Getty Images
What is Nubank, and why does Brazil's election matter for it?

Nubank is one of Latin America's largest digital banking platforms, offering credit cards, personal loans, savings accounts, and other financial services.

Founded in Brazil in 2013, the company has expanded into Mexico and Colombia. Its business is particularly sensitive to changes in interest rates, consumer spending, and borrowing costs.

Brazil has struggled with persistent fiscal deficits, rising public debt, and inflation, and Lula's victory has raised concerns about Brazil's fiscal outlook, potential tax increases, and greater government intervention in the economy.

Guilherme Abbud, CEO of Persevera Asset Management, said the Brazilian real could weaken by at least 7% following the election.

Key Takeaways

Petrobras fell 15% today after Lula won Sunday's runoff in Brazil with 51.8% of the vote. MercadoLibre, Ambev and LATAM Airlines also fell.

The government controls Petrobras, so a fourth Lula term keeps the same people in charge of its spending and dividends.

Petrobras's capital spending has more than doubled since 2022, and over the same years its dividends have fallen from 94% of free cash flow to under 40%.

Watch Petrobras's third-quarter report in the coming weeks for signs of whether the dividend holds up.

Investors were betting that Bolsonaro would win in Brazil. They lost that bet, and Petrobras (PBR) is down 15% this morning.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Sunday's runoff with 51.8% of the vote to Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.2%, weeks after losing the first round. No Brazilian candidate had ever lost the first round and gone on to win the final.

US-listed Brazilian stocks fell across the board. MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ), whose biggest market is Brazil, fell 12%, Ambev (ABEV) fell 12%, and Chile's LATAM Airlines (LTM), with its big Brazilian domestic business, fell 9%.

Petrobras answers to Brasília

The government controls Petrobras, so the vote decides who sets its priorities for four more years. And Lula's current term, which began in 2023, already shows what those priorities look like.

Petrobras's capital spending has more than doubled since 2022…

Petróleo Brasileiro S.A. – Petrobras (PBR): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

…while its free cash flow has fallen by more than half, and the dividends it pays out of that cash have shrunk even faster:

Petróleo Brasileiro S.A. – Petrobras (PBR): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

In 2022, Jair Bolsonaro's last year in office, dividends ate up 94% of free cash flow. In 2024 and 2025, they took under 40%. Investors had been betting a Bolsonaro win would turn that around. Another Lula term looks like more of the same.

The multiple can go lower

Before today, Petrobras traded at 4.5x forward earnings, a bit above its five-year average of 4.0x…

At this morning's price, it's closer to 3.6x, about half its April high of 7.3x. But the five-year low, 1.5x, came on Jan. 3, 2023, two days after Lula's third term began.

The rest of the group fell on country risk. For MercadoLibre and Ambev, a 10% drop in the real, which reports say is possible, would shrink what their Brazilian sales are worth in dollars. LATAM fell less: it's a Chilean airline, and Brazil is only part of its business.

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI continues to strengthen its position in Latin America's e-commerce market, supported by expanding buyer engagement, competitive pricing, and logistics investments. Its growing marketplace scale and efforts to improve the shopping experience are helping the company attract customers and deepen its presence across key markets.

The momentum was evident in second-quarter 2026 results, with gross merchandise volume (GMV) rising 44% year over year to $21.9 billion, or 36% on an FX-neutral basis. Items sold increased 45%, while unique active buyers climbed 26% to 89.3 million. Items purchased per buyer grew 14%, reflecting stronger engagement.

Brazil remains a key growth engine. The lower free-shipping threshold continued to support demand, with FX-neutral GMV increasing 39% and items sold rising 56%. Conversion improved 1.1 percentage points year over year. MercadoLibre also introduced buyer discounts for PIX payments and reduced seller take rates in selected categories, improving price competitiveness and helping active sellers grow 29%.

Broader product availability and faster delivery further reinforce its competitive position. Cross-border trade GMV increased 60% on an FX-neutral basis, while same-day and next-day shipments rose 38% to 225 million.

However, weaker consumer demand in Mexico and Argentina presents challenges to maintaining growth momentum. MercadoLibre's ability to sustain engagement, competitive pricing and service improvements will remain important to expanding its marketplace leadership.

MercadoLibre, which competes with Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN and Sea Limited SE, has seen its shares decline 0.5% over the past three months against the industry's 2.3% growth. While Amazon shares have climbed 7.2%, Sea Limited has fallen 28.5% in the aforementioned period.

Brazil's surprise election result is hitting the country's U.S.-listed companies hardest where government policy and borrowing costs carry the most weight. rocharibeiro/Shutterstock.com

Meanwhile, Petrobras (NYSE:PBR) stock is sliding 21% to $20.54, trailing only Nu Holdings among the three companies, as the state-controlled oil producer faces fresh questions about government influence. MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) shares are falling 15% to $1,545, a smaller decline than either Nu Holdings or Petrobras.

The selling pressure is landing directly on Brazil. Tracking a broad basket of Brazilian equities, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (NYSEARCA:EWZ) is down 28% to $30.66, a deeper slide than any of the three companies. For comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.3% to $762.13, showing that risk appetite outside of Brazil is holding steady.

Lula's Fourth-Term Upset Catches Markets Off Guard

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidential runoff over the weekend, a surprise victory that gives him a fourth term and sends a shock through Nu Holdings, Petrobras and MercadoLibre shares. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who led the first round earlier this month, has refused to concede, adding further political uncertainty.

------

Investors had largely positioned for a Bolsonaro win and the economic reforms it was expected to bring. Brazil is dealing with deteriorating public finances and elevated interest rates. Nu Holdings and Petrobras Absorb the Heaviest Blows

Nu Holdings is a digital financial services platform operating primarily in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia, with the majority of its customers in Brazil. That footprint ties the company directly to Brazilian interest rates, consumer credit conditions and the tax treatment of financial services. Lula's win stokes fears of further tax hikes and heavier regulation on Brazilian lenders, and as a result Nu Holdings stock is leading the decline.

Petrobras is Brazil's state-controlled integrated oil company, with the national government as its controlling shareholder. Such a structure makes the oil producer sharply sensitive to the presidency, with the selloff reflecting fears of renewed state intervention, fuel-price controls, higher taxation, and dividend policy risk. A new crude export tax and fuel subsidy obligations already weigh on the company, though its large deepwater and pre-salt production base still gives Petrobras a solid operating foundation.

MercadoLibre runs e-commerce and fintech businesses across Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and other Latin American markets. Yet, Brazil is its largest market, which leaves the company highly sensitive to a weaker real and local policy risk. Its wider reach hasn't saved it a steep decline, though MercadoLibre stock is holding up better than the two names most tied to Brasília.

Next up for MercadoLibre is its quarterly report, expected in early November, though the company hasn't yet confirmed the date. That report is the next test of whether Brazilian demand holds up after the election. Steady order growth in the results could help MercadoLibre stock separate from the wider Brazil selloff.

For Nu Holdings and Petrobras, the clearest signals could come from how quickly Lula's government outlines its fiscal repair plan and from fresh tax measures on Brazilian financial services. Any shift in Petrobras' pricing or dividend policy could also sway its shares.

With the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF falling harder than any single company, the political shock is clearly spreading across the country's equities. title: Is It Worth Investing in MercadoLibre (MELI) Based on Wall Street's Bullish Views?

The recommendations of Wall Street analysts are often relied on by investors when deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock. Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though?

Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about MercadoLibre (MELI) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage.

MercadoLibre currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.45, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 19 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.45 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 19 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 14 are Strong Buy and one is Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 73.7% and 5.3% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for MELI

Check price target & stock forecast for MercadoLibre here>>>

While the ABR calls for buying MercadoLibre, it may not be wise to make an investment decision solely based on this information. Several studies have shown limited to no success of brokerage recommendations in guiding investors to pick stocks with the best price increase potential.

Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.

This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR

In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.

Broker recommendations are the sole basis for calculating the ABR, which is typically displayed in decimals (such as 1.28). The Zacks Rank, on the other hand, is a quantitative model designed to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

Analysts employed by brokerage firms have been and continue to be overly optimistic with their recommendations. Since the ratings issued by these analysts are more favorable than their research would support because of the vested interest of their employers, they mislead investors far more often than they guide.

On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

Furthermore, the different grades of the Zacks Rank are applied proportionately across all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide earnings estimates for the current year. In other words, at all times, this tool maintains a balance among the five ranks it assigns.

There is also a key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank when it comes to freshness. When you look at the ABR, it may not be up-to-date. Nonetheless, since brokerage analysts constantly revise their earnings estimates to reflect changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in predicting future stock prices.

Should You Invest in MELI?

Looking at the earnings estimate revisions for MercadoLibre, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current year has declined 2.6% over the past month to $38.09.

Analysts' growing pessimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates lower, could be a legitimate reason for the stock to plunge in the near term.

The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #4 (Sell) for MercadoLibre. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) stocks here >>>>

Therefore, it could be wise to take the Buy-equivalent ABR for MercadoLibre with a grain of salt.

MercadoLibre recently rolled out one hour delivery in São Paulo and moved into selling prescription medicines in Brazil, while also raising US$1b in long term notes to support logistics and credit operations, alongside quarterly revenue growth paired with weaker operating income and margins.

The combination of faster delivery promises and higher capital spending highlights a trade off between building scale in Brazil and near term pressure on MercadoLibre's profitability profile.

We will now explore how MercadoLibre's investment narrative is affected by this push into one hour delivery and prescription medicine sales.

Compare MercadoLibre's push into faster delivery with a curated set of logistics heavyweights and capital disciplined platforms in our list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (25 results).

MercadoLibre Investment Narrative Recap

To own MercadoLibre, you need to believe that its heavy reinvestment in logistics, payments and credit eventually supports healthier unit economics rather than leaving margins under pressure. The recent launch of one hour delivery and prescription drug sales in Brazil pushes more volume into an already dense network. The short term swing factor is margin stabilization, since Q2 already showed weaker operating income.

The biggest risk right now sits in the combination of thinner profitability and a growing credit book funded with a high level of debt. Faster shipping and a broader assortment do not change that risk directly, but they can add complexity if higher volumes coincide with softer credit quality or prolonged higher shipping and marketing costs.

The most relevant recent move for this story is the US$1b long term notes issue. That funding is earmarked for logistics and credit growth, which ties directly into one hour delivery promises and the broader MercadoLibre ecosystem. Extra liquidity gives the business more room to keep free shipping thresholds low and expand first party assortment while maintaining its fulfillment build out.

The trade off is that more borrowing adds to an already leveraged balance sheet. For you as a shareholder, the key question is whether incremental returns from denser logistics and a larger US$16.4b credit book offset higher interest expense and the risk of future credit losses. Those outcomes feed straight into the margin path that many investors are watching closely over the next few years.

MercadoLibre's narrative projects US$75.8b revenue and US$5.2b earnings by 2029. This aligns with analysts assuming 29.1% yearly revenue growth and implies earnings need to rise by about US$3.3b from US$1.9b today.

Instead, they are questioning how long margins stay under pressure.

The latest move is a speed play. MercadoLibre launched deliveries within one hour in São Paulo for items up to 15 kilograms, including food and medications. It also began selling prescription medicines through its own São Paulo pharmacy and targets 20 partner locations by year-end. Timing matters here, since Sea's Shopee launched four-hour delivery in Brazil in August.

Q2 results show the trade-off clearly. Net revenue jumped 50% to $10.2 billion, topping $10 billion for the first time. However, operating income fell 17% to $683 million, and operating margin compressed 5.5 percentage points to 6.7%. Net income dropped 11% to $466 million, marking a third straight quarter of year-over-year declines.

CEO Ariel Szarfsztejn described AI as "accelerating the secular shift we already are trying to capture," pointing to better search and lending decisions. The company also raised $1 billion in 10-year notes at a coupon near 5.9%, which strengthens liquidity for logistics and credit growth. Going forward, MELI stock likely hinges on whether Q3 shows margins stabilizing while growth stays above 40%.

Margins Are the Whole Valuation Debate
MELI Guided Valuation Model (TIKR)

Under valuation model assumptions realized through 12/31/28, the stock is modeled using:

Revenue Growth (CAGR): 32.4%

Operating Margins: 8.3%

Exit P/E Multiple: 40.6x

Based on these inputs, the model estimates a target price of $3,846, implying a 109.7% total return from the current share price of $1,834 and an annualized return of 39.8% over the next 2.2 years.

This is a margin compression story with a recovery bet attached. MercadoLibre's operating margin was 12.7% over the past year in the model, but Q2 slipped to 6.7% as free shipping and credit spending ramped up. The model assumes 8.3%, which equals the trailing margin today. So the forecast needs no full rebound, just no further damage.

MELI Guided Valuation Model (TIKR)

Growth assumptions look conservative against the company's record. Revenue grew 39.1% over the last year and 48.7% annually over five years, while analysts expect about 36.9% over the next two years. The model's 32.4% input therefore leaves a cushion. Mercado Pago's credit book, up 75% to $16.4 billion, keeps feeding that top line.

The 40.6x exit multiple matches the past year's P/E and sits well below the 64.3x five-year average. Today's forward P/E, the price paid for each $1 of next year's expected profit, is near 43.5x. That means the model actually assumes slight compression. A 39.8% annual return is exceptional, but it depends on the investment cycle paying off while Sea Limited (SE) keeps pricing pressure on Brazil.

Shopee Is Chasing MercadoLibre Into Brazil

Sea Limited (SE), owner of Shopee, is MercadoLibre's most aggressive rival in Brazil. Sea's Q2 revenue rose 48.1% to $7.8 billion, nearly matching MercadoLibre's 50% growth. Shopee's gross merchandise volume (GMV), the total value of goods sold, grew 28.4% to $38.3 billion. Sea's management also called Brazil its fastest-growing market in the quarter.

Fintech is a head-to-head race too. Sea's lending arm, Monee, grew revenue 58.9% to $1.4 billion, with loans outstanding up 62.5% to $11.1 billion. Mercado Pago's credit portfolio is larger at $16.4 billion and growing faster at 75%. That lead gives MercadoLibre more data to price risk, which supports credit margins.

Profitability shows where the money goes. Shopee earned $255.4 million in adjusted EBITDA on $5.6 billion of revenue, a margin of roughly 4.6%. Although the measures differ, MercadoLibre's 6.7% operating margin remains higher even after this year's spending. Amazon (AMZN) also competes in Brazil and Mexico, yet MercadoLibre's moat is its owned logistics network, which delivered 77% of fast shipments in Brazil within 48 hours.

*__Weigh the projected EBIT turnaround against three straight quarters of profit declines >>>__*

What's Driving MELI Stock Going Forward?

Q3 results on November 2 come first. Investors want to see whether operating margin holds near Q2's 6.7% or slips again. The Q2 shareholder letter described the squeeze as a deliberate choice to reinvest efficiency gains into the customer offer. So any commentary on shipping subsidies will matter as much as revenue.

Brazil's quick commerce push is the near-term swing factor. One-hour delivery and pharmacy sales increase how often customers open the app, which lifts order frequency and advertising value. These services also require more fulfillment centers and couriers, so costs arrive before revenue. Past cuts to seller shipping fees in 2024 and 2025 followed the same pattern and strengthened engagement.

Credit remains the profit engine. Net interest margin after losses, a measure of lending profit after bad loans, improved from 18% in Q1 to 21% in Q2. Mercado Pago is also expanding its credit card business despite concerns about Brazilian consumer debt. Fresh bond funding gives MercadoLibre room to keep growing that book through 2027.
